areas.title: Foreground toolkit

areas.title: Site UI
areas.blurb: The site's own button, pill, section header and data panel.

areas.title: Page
areas.blurb: The data-driven page: hero, twenty block types and the template that renders them.

areas.title: Shell
areas.blurb: The frame around every page: navbar, footer, search, shortcuts, cursor, route transitions, effects.

areas.title: Reveal & kinetic type
areas.blurb: Entrance animation: 33 reveal profiles and the kinetic text engine.

areas.title: Scenes
areas.blurb: The Canvas scene host and the library of 67 background scenes.

areas.title: Signatures

areas.title: Closers

areas.title: Specimens

areas.title: Stage

areas.title: Core
areas.blurb: Hooks, providers, the motion engine, utilities and site sources.

split.label: Pinned left
split.hint: The left side holds still and moves with you; the right column scrolls.

splitR.label: Pinned right
splitR.hint: The right side holds still and moves with you; the left column scrolls.

index.label: Live index
index.hint: An index follows you down the left while each specimen takes a full screen.

counter.label: Counter-scroll
counter.hint: Two columns drift in opposite directions as you scroll.

rail.label: Sideways rail
rail.hint: Scrolling down drives a track sideways past a fixed panel.

stack.label: Sticky stack
stack.hint: Specimens pile up like a deck of cards.

orbit.label: Centre stage
orbit.hint: A still centre; specimens arrive from both sides.

spine.label: Spine
spine.hint: A line fills as you scroll and specimens branch from it.

wheel.label: Carousel
wheel.hint: Specimens ride a ring that turns with the page.

tunnel.label: Fly-through
tunnel.hint: The camera moves forward through a column of specimens.

slides.label: Wipes
slides.hint: One specimen at a time, cut in by a moving edge.

columns.label: Parallax
columns.hint: Columns move at different speeds beside a fixed panel.

map.label: Pan map
map.hint: The page pans across a large field along a path.

canvas.label: Canvas flight
canvas.hint: The page is a canvas: scrolling pulls the camera out, flies it left, right, up or down to the next specimen, and drops it back in.

atlas.label: Atlas
atlas.hint: Every specimen sits on one sheet. The camera dives into each, and at the end of every row pulls right out to show the whole sheet.

spiral.label: Spiral
spiral.hint: The specimens wind outward in a spiral and the camera follows them round, banking as it turns.

families.title: Switchboard
families.line: Forty ways to flip a state.
families.blurb: Switches, latches and breakers on a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description:
01 · SWITCHBOARD — forty ways to flip a state.
The still side is the board itself: forty lamps, one per specimen, that
light as the page passes them while a scan line sweeps the grid.

families.title: Dials
families.blurb: Knobs, wheels and rotaries wound out along a spiral.
families.description:
02 · DIALS — turn, wind, spin and detent.
The still centre is a dial of its own: a bezel that turns two full revolutions
against a needle that sweeps the other way, with an arc that draws as you go.

families.title: Faders
families.line: Sliders on a rail that slides.
families.blurb: Ranges, scrubbers and tracks on a sideways rail.
families.description:
03 · FADERS — sliders on a rail that slides.
The still side is an eight-channel desk whose caps ride the scroll.

families.title: Keypads
families.line: Keys, triggers and buttons with a feel.
families.blurb: Press mechanics in three parallax columns.
families.description:
04 · KEYPADS — keys, triggers and buttons with a feel.
The still side is a backlit key matrix; a wave of light and a press travels
across it as the page scrolls.

families.title: Fields
families.blurb: Text, date, code and tag fields beside a live index.
families.description:
05 · FIELDS — inputs, pickers and steppers, reimagined.
The still side is a form that fills itself in, row by row, as you read.

families.title: Gauges
families.blurb: Needles, arcs and bars wound out along a spiral.
families.description:
06 · GAUGES — meters that read the room.
The pinned side is a dial stack that the scroll alone drives: three arcs fill
at different rates, a ring of dashes turns, a needle trembles toward 100, and
the number in the middle is written by CSS counters — no script per frame.
Angles throughout run clockwise from twelve o'clock.

families.title: Charts
families.blurb: Forty small charts on one sheet; the camera dives into each.
families.description:
07 · CHARTS — marks, bars, lines and areas.
The still middle of the page is a plotter: a line is drawn down the screen as
you scroll, two series, a crosshair and a dot per series — the dots and the
numbers beside them come from the same sine sums the paths were drawn with, so
CSS (sin, counters) and SVG agree without any script per frame.
Every sample is generated from a seed, so a chart is the same on every render.

families.title: Matrices
families.line: Heat, tables and dot grids to pan across.
families.blurb: Heat, tables and dot grids on one sheet you fly across.
families.description:
08 · MATRICES — heat, tables and dot grids to pan across.
The page is a field of forty-two grids you travel across along a snaking path.
On the left, a small map of that field: the red cell and the dot are where the
scroll has taken you, the line is the way so far, and the numbers beside them
are written by CSS counters — the same `--pin` that moves the field draws them.
Most specimens below are grids read with the pointer or the arrow keys
(useCell); the rest are small games, tables and displays.

families.title: Figures
families.line: Numerals that roll, flip and settle.
families.blurb: Counters and clocks cut in one at a time.
families.description:
09 · FIGURES — numerals that roll, flip and settle.
One specimen fills the right of the screen at a time, cut in by a moving edge.
On the left, two odometers read the scroll itself: the big one counts which
specimen you are on, the small one how far down the page you are. They are
rolling reels of digits moved by CSS (round / mod on the scroll number), with
the carry behaving like a real odometer: a digit only turns over while the
one beside it is passing nine.

families.title: Graphs
families.line: Nodes, trees and flows that grow.
families.blurb: Networks that branch from a filling spine.
families.description:
10 · GRAPHS — nodes, trees and flows that grow.
A spine runs down the middle of the page and specimens branch off it. The disc
that rides the spine is a graph of its own: thirty-one nodes appear one by one
as you scroll, each link drawing itself from its parent, and the counters in
the middle are written by CSS. Everything below is a graph of some kind —
trees, networks, flows, fractals — drawn from fixed data, so it is the same
on every render.

families.title: Kinetic
families.line: Words that scramble, split and settle.
families.blurb: Moving type on a canvas the camera swoops across.
families.description:
11 · KINETIC — words that scramble, split and settle.
The still side is one enormous letter. As you scroll it steps through the
alphabet, and between two letters each is cut in half across the middle: the
halves slide apart in opposite directions as one fades out and the next slides
together. The numbers that drive it are the page's --f, read by CSS.
Everything below is a line of moving type; the ones that react to the pointer
work from the keyboard too.

families.title: Tickers
families.blurb: Mechanical text on belts that slide both ways.
families.description:
12 · TICKERS — flaps, boards and marquees.
The still side is a split-flap board. Every flap is a scroll-driven counter:
CSS reads the page's --pin, turns it into "which letter, and how far through
the flip", prints the letters with counters (upper-alpha, decimal) and tilts
the two moving halves by that fraction. Nothing is animated by script.
Everything on the right is a belt, a board or a sign.

families.title: Markup
families.blurb: Annotations that stack like pages in a deck.
families.description:
13 · MARKUP — highlights, strikes and redactions.
The still side is a page of notes. As you scroll, a pen goes through it: a
phrase is highlighted, another crossed out, a word circled, a few lines blacked
out. Each mark has a progress of its own (--m, from the page's --pin and the
mark's order) and CSS draws it; nothing is animated by script.
Everything in the deck is something you can do to a line of text.

families.title: Glyphs
families.blurb: Letterforms riding a carousel ring.
families.description:
14 · GLYPHS — outlines, strokes and letterforms.
The still side is a type specimen sheet: one huge glyph at a time, drawn
against the five lines every letter lives between (ascender, cap height,
x-height, baseline, descender). The scroll outlines the glyph, then a scan
line fills it from the top; the next glyph takes over. The metrics are the
real ones for the site's serif. Everything is CSS reading the page's --pin.
The ring carries forty-two things you can do to a letter.

families.title: Editorial
families.blurb: Editorial parts met on a fly-through.
families.description:
15 · EDITORIAL — quotes, captions and footnotes.
The still side is a magazine page that sets itself as you scroll: a kicker,
a headline that rises line by line, a standfirst that wipes in, two columns of
text filling line by line, a pull quote, a figure, a footnote. Each part has a
window of the scroll and CSS reads it from the page's --pin.
What flies past is the furniture of a page of editorial.

families.title: Tilt
families.blurb: Parallax and tilt surfaces in a deep column.
families.description:
16 · TILT — cards with depth and weight.
The still side is an exploded module in isometric view. Its six layers pull
apart along the vertical axis and close again as you scroll, and the whole
thing turns a quarter: the gap is sin(pin × π), the turn is pin, both in CSS.
Forty-two cards ride the fly-through, each doing something with perspective.

families.title: Glow
families.line: Spotlights, beams and borders of light.
families.blurb: Light-led cards on a dark canvas, found by flying across it.
families.description:
17 · GLOW — spotlights, beams and borders of light.
The still side is a pendant lamp that swings over a row of tiles. Where the
cone falls a tile lights up: border, fill, glow and lift. Both the swing and the
cone are one number — the beam's position, sin(pin × 4π) — and CSS does the
rest (atan2 for the lamp's angle, a clip-path for the cone, clamp for how lit
each tile is). Forty-two cards on the left are each lit in their own way.

families.title: Fold
families.line: Cards that flip, fold and peel.
families.blurb: Turning, folding cards on a rotating ring.
families.description:
18 · FOLD — cards that flip, fold and peel.
The still side is a leaflet of four panels. Each panel hangs from the one
before it, and each hinge turns by the same --fold (times 1, -2, 2: that is what
makes it an accordion). The scroll opens it flat, holds it, and folds it the
other way. The turning ring on the right holds forty-two things to flip, fold,
peel and tear.

families.title: Bento
families.blurb: Dashboard tiles on one sheet, dived into one by one.
families.description:
19 · BENTO — tiles that tessellate.
The still side is one board of eight tiles that settles into three different
arrangements as you scroll. Each tile has a rectangle in each arrangement, and
its box is a blend of the three, weighted by two eased numbers taken from --pin:
plain calc(), no script. On the right, forty-two dashboard tiles drift in two
columns, each one a small working thing.

families.title: Passes
families.blurb: Perforated passes scattered over a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description:
20 · PASSES — tickets, receipts and badges.
A line runs down the middle of the page and a pass hangs from either side of it.
The medallion that rides the line is a pass of its own: a code prints itself row
by row as you scroll, a ring of forty-two punch holes fills one for each pass
you have passed, and the counter in the middle is written by CSS. Everything
below is something you could be handed at a door — boarding passes to tear,
stamps to land, codes to scan, badges to swing.

families.title: Tabs
families.line: Strips, pills and segments that glide.
families.blurb: Tab systems beside a live index.
families.description:
21 · TABS — strips, pills and segments that glide.
The still side is a strip of five tabs whose underline is driven by the
scroll alone: it slides along the strip, the label it reaches lights, and a
panel title below it follows. Specimens share one small tablist (roving
tabindex, arrow keys, Home and End), so every one of them works from a keyboard.

families.title: Docks
families.blurb: Bars and rails on a canvas the camera flies across.
families.description:
22 · DOCKS — floating bars, rails and toolbars.
The still side is a dock of seven discs with the classic magnification, but
driven by the scroll: a swell travels along the row as the page moves, so
the disc under the "cursor" rises and its neighbours follow.

families.title: Menus
families.blurb: Menu forms around a pinned node map.
families.description:
23 · MENUS — dropdowns, radials and command lists.
The still side is a node map: a hub and seven stops joined by lines. The
scroll opens one stop at a time (a petal lifts and its line fills) while a
pulse runs out along the line to it. Specimens share a tiny open/close hook
(Escape and an outside press close a menu) and are operable by keyboard.

families.title: Steps
families.blurb: Sequences along a sideways rail.
families.description:
24 · STEPS — steppers, breadcrumbs and pagination.
The still side is a winding path: a line that draws itself as the page
scrolls, a marker that rides it, and five waypoints that light as it passes.
Specimens share nothing but good manners: every stepper can be moved from
the keyboard and says where it is in words.

families.title: Waypoints
families.blurb: Wayfinding pieces on an atlas you fly across.
families.description:
25 · WAYPOINTS — outlines, contents and wayfinding.
The still side is a compass: a needle that turns twice over the journey and
eight waypoints around the dial that light as it passes. Specimens are the
other ways a page tells you where you are and where to go next.

families.title: Loaders
families.blurb: Spinners and waiting states wound out along a spiral.
families.description:
26 · LOADERS — forty ways to wait.
Nearly everything here runs by itself, and only while it is on screen (the
specimen frame pauses every animation that is off-screen). The still side is
a core with five rings that the scroll turns at five speeds, so the page
itself is the thing being waited on.

families.title: Toasts
families.blurb: Notices that arrive and pile up.
families.description:
27 · TOASTS — alerts, banners and notices.
The still side is a stack of five notices that arrive one by one as the page
scrolls: each slides in on its --f and the ones before it shrink back, as
a real stack does. Specimens use a small queue (auto-dismiss that pauses
under the pointer or focus) and announce themselves politely to a screen reader.

families.title: Progress
families.line: Bars, rings and vessels that fill.
families.blurb: Fills and meters in counter-scrolling columns.
families.description:
28 · PROGRESS — bars, rings and vessels that fill.
Most specimens are pure CSS: one registered number, --v (0 to 1), is run by a
keyframe animation and every bar, ring and counter below reads it, so they
all fill in step with their own clock. The ones that answer to you are the
sliders, the uploads and the buttons. The still side is a ring and three bars
that the scroll itself fills, with the figure written by CSS counters.

families.title: Skeletons
families.blurb: Waiting shapes cut in one at a time.
families.description:
29 · SKELETONS — placeholders and empty states.
The still side is one card that resolves as you scroll: grey bars sharpen
into a heading, a line of text and a figure at the scroll's own pace (every
step is a CSS number, so nothing re-renders). Specimens are the waiting
shapes — and what a page says when there is nothing to wait for.

families.title: Signals
families.blurb: Status lights beside a pinned beacon.
families.description:
30 · SIGNALS — lights, pills and health.
The still side is a beacon whose colour is the scroll's progress: it goes
from green to amber to red as the page is read, its rings widen and the word
under it changes with it. Specimens are the other ways a thing can say how
it is — and each one says it in words as well as in light.

families.title: Popovers
families.blurb: Anchored overlays with a pinned reference.
families.description:
31 · POPOVERS — tooltips, hover cards and callouts.
The still side is a reference square with one popover that walks round it:
the scroll sets its angle, so over the page it takes up every placement in
turn, its arrow turning to keep pointing home. Specimens use a tiny open /
close hook (Escape and an outside press close one) and every tooltip opens on
keyboard focus as well as on hover.

families.title: Sheets
families.blurb: Layered panes met on a fly-through.
families.description:
32 · SHEETS — drawers, modals and layered panes.
The still side is a stack of five panes in depth: the scroll slides them
apart along the view axis, each lifting out of the pile in turn, the way
layers come apart in a design tool. Every specimen lives in a small stage of
its own (so a "full screen" sheet only fills its box), traps nothing,
and closes with its own button or Escape.

families.title: Cursors
families.blurb: Pointer effects across a canvas the camera flies over.
families.description:
33 · CURSORS — pointers, followers and magnets.
Every specimen is an area that publishes two numbers, --x and --y (0 to 1,
where the pointer is), and CSS does the rest — a follower is a transition
with a lag, a trail is the same dot with longer lags, a magnet is a
translate. Nothing re-renders as the pointer moves. When nobody is pointing,
a virtual pointer wanders on a slow curve (while the specimen is on screen,
never under reduced motion) so the effect is always visible; the arrow keys
move it by hand.
The still side is the same idea driven by the page: a cursor rides a figure
of eight, trailing ghosts, as the scroll moves.

families.title: Wipes
families.blurb: Transitions cut in by a moving edge.
families.description:
34 · WIPES — curtains, clips and reveals.
A wipe is a rule for how panel B replaces panel A, so nearly every specimen
is the same two panels and a different rule. Press one to run it; until
someone does, each runs itself now and then while it is on screen (never under
reduced motion). The still side is one wipe, scrubbed by the scroll: a clip
edge sweeps across a pair of panels from first to last.

families.title: Lenses
families.blurb: Lenses on belts that slide both ways.
families.description:
35 · LENSES — magnifiers, compare and focus.
A lens shows the same thing twice, once as it is and once changed, and lets
the pointer decide where. Most specimens publish the pointer as --x / --y
(pointerVars.js) and draw a second, changed copy of the picture clipped to
a shape that sits on it; a wandering virtual pointer keeps them moving until
you take over. The still side is one lens that the scroll carries across a
page of small type, enlarging whatever it passes.

families.title: Cockpit
families.blurb: Flight instruments on a rotating ring.
families.description:
36 · COCKPIT — instruments with presence.
Sixteen of the forty-two are one dial component given sixteen faces (a
range, a sweep, coloured bands, a redline): every needle can be dragged, and
until you do, each wanders between readings by itself while it is on screen.
The rest are the instruments a dial cannot be — a horizon, a compass card, a
lever, a tape. The still side is a heading card that the scroll turns twice.

families.title: Studio
families.line: Meters, reels and faders for sound.
families.blurb: Studio gear beside a pinned VU needle.
families.description:
37 · STUDIO — meters, reels and faders for sound.
Nothing here makes a sound: these are the faces of studio gear. The still
side is a VU meter whose needle follows a swinging signal that the scroll
scrubs — a loud passage, a quiet one, a peak. Specimens that would be moving
in a studio move by themselves while on screen (never under reduced motion),
and the ones you operate are real controls with values you can read.

families.title: Terminal
families.blurb: Console parts with a live index.
families.description:
38 · TERMINAL — pieces of a command line.
Everything is drawn in text. The still side is a console window that prints
a build log line by line as the scroll advances; the forty-two specimens
beside it are prompts, logs, diffs and menus. The ones that would be running
run by themselves while on screen (never under reduced motion), and the ones
that take input are real inputs and buttons with the keys you would expect.

families.title: Stamps
families.blurb: Marks pressed onto a canvas, found one by one.
families.description:
39 · STAMPS — marks pressed onto paper: labels, seals, stickers and tape.
The still side is a large APPROVED stamp coming down onto paper as the
scroll advances (it lands at the middle of the page and the ink spreads
after). The forty-two specimens are the things you would find on a desk:
most can be pressed, peeled or torn with a click, and every one is a button
or a field you can reach with the keyboard.

families.title: Archive
families.blurb: Records filed in a sticky deck.
families.description:
40 · ARCHIVE — files, drawers and index cards.
The still side is a card drawer: a row of index cards that slides past as
the scroll advances, the one in front turning to face you. The forty-two
specimens are the furniture of a records room. Most of them open, pull out or
turn over with a click; every one is a button or a field, so the keyboard
reaches them all.

families.title: Beams
families.blurb: Light traces running along a spine.
families.description:
41 · BEAMS — lines and traces of light.
The still side is a circuit trace that runs the length of the page: a pulse
of light travels along it as the scroll advances and the pads it passes light
up behind it. The forty-two specimens are swatches of light on a dark ground:
traces, tubes, rays and sweeps. The ones that would be moving are, while on
screen (never under reduced motion); the rest answer to the pointer, a drag
or a click, and all of them can be reached from the keyboard.

families.title: Patterns
families.line: Grids, dots and hatching as surfaces.
families.blurb: Surfaces laid out on one sheet.
families.description:
42 · PATTERNS — grids, dots and hatching as surfaces.
The still side is a sheet whose surface changes as the scroll advances: a
field of dots grows, then gives way to hatching from the left. The forty-two
specimens are swatches. Thirty of them are drawn with nothing but gradients
and inline SVG tiles (so they cost no images); the rest move, follow the
pointer or take a slider, and every control can be reached from the keyboard.

families.title: Drift
families.blurb: Particle systems wound out along a spiral.
families.description:
43 · DRIFT — particles, stars and rain.
The still side is a spiral of dots that winds up as the scroll advances.
Each of the forty-two specimens is a small particle system drawn on its own
canvas. A system only runs while it is on screen, and under reduced motion it
draws one settled frame and stops. Where the pointer matters it is the
pointer (or the arrow keys, with Enter to act), so a keyboard reaches them all.

families.title: Waves
families.blurb: Wave forms on sliding belts.
families.description:
44 · WAVES — ripples, interference and noise.
The still side is two sets of rings that spread apart as the scroll advances,
so the pattern where they overlap shifts. Each of the forty-two specimens is
a wave drawn on its own canvas through the shared Sim engine (Sim.jsx): it
runs only while on screen, draws one settled frame under reduced motion, and
where the pointer matters it is the pointer, or the arrow keys with Enter.

families.title: Morphs
families.blurb: Shape-changers scattered across a canvas.
families.description:
45 · MORPHS — shapes that become other shapes.
The still side is one shape that is a circle at the top of the page, a star in
the middle and a square at the end, with every point of its outline sliding
between them as the scroll advances. The forty-two specimens change shape
too: by sliding the points of a clipped outline (the same trick), by CSS
radii and transforms, by tweening the numbers of an SVG, or by melting
together through a blur-and-threshold filter. Each one changes when you click,
hover or slide it, or by itself while on screen.

families.title: Handset
families.blurb: Phone-screen patterns beside a pinned handset.
families.description:
46 · HANDSET — mobile screens, from first run to settings.
The still side is a phone whose screen slides through five states as the
scroll advances: welcome, sign in, a feed, a chat and settings. Each of the
forty-two specimens is a small screen of the same kind, drawn at phone
proportions: the ones you would tap are real buttons, fields and switches
that work, and the ones that would run on their own do so while on screen.

families.title: Boards
families.blurb: Planning surfaces on one sheet.
families.description:
47 · BOARDS — kanban, calendars and agendas on one sheet.
The still side is a three-lane board whose cards move across it as the scroll
advances: from To do, through Doing, to Done. The forty-two specimens are
planning surfaces of the same kind, small enough to sit on one sheet and
working: cards move when you click them, days and slots select, and the
boards that would be ticking over (a countdown, a focus timer) do so while
they are on screen.

families.title: Feeds
families.blurb: Streams and lists with a live index.
families.description:
48 · FEEDS — lists, chats and notification streams.
The still side is a chat stream that scrolls past as the scroll advances,
the message in the middle of the frame lit and the ones leaving it fading
out. The forty-two specimens are the parts of a stream: list rows you pick,
reorder or expand, chat bubbles and their small furniture, and the ways a
notification arrives and goes. Everything that takes input is a real button
or field, and the streams that would be arriving do so while on screen.

families.title: Checkout
families.blurb: Sample pricing and order parts in parallax columns.
families.description:
49 · CHECKOUT — pricing, carts and order flows.
The still side is a receipt that prints as the scroll advances: a line
appears for each item, then the total underlines itself. The forty-two
specimens are the parts of buying something: plan cards and toggles, cart
lines and shipping, the steps of paying, and what comes after. The prices are
made up, but every control does its sum: change a quantity, a plan or a tip
and the totals follow. Nothing is sent anywhere.

families.title: Heroes
families.blurb: Layouts for opening screens, scattered across a canvas.
families.description:
50 · HEROES — opening screens, bands and endings.
The still side is one hero that re-lays itself out as the scroll advances:
the headline slides left while a shape grows in on the right and the button
settles beneath. The forty-two specimens are layouts of the same kind, drawn
small: openings of every shape, the bands that sit between sections, and the
endings that close a page. Each has one thing you can do to it (press,
type, hover, switch) or does something by itself while on screen.

entries.name: Checkbox
entries.summary: A checkbox with room for a hint. It is a real input — the square is drawn beside it — and it supports the indeterminate “some of them” state of a parent box.

props.name: hint
props.description: A smaller line under the label.

props.name: indeterminate
props.description: The mixed state of a parent whose children differ.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

notes: Indeterminate is a display state only: it becomes checked or unchecked when pressed.
The whole label is the click target.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Checkbox label="Send the weekly summary" checked={on} onChange={setOn} />

entries.name: Combobox
entries.summary: An editable combobox: type to filter, move through the matches with the arrow keys, choose with Enter. Focus stays in the input; the highlighted option is named with aria-activedescendant.
entries.description:
An editable combobox (the ARIA 1.2 list-autocomplete pattern): type to filter,
↓ ↑ to move through the matches, Home and End to jump, Enter to choose, Escape
to close — and then to clear. DOM focus stays in the input; the highlighted
option is named with `aria-activedescendant`.

options: ['Cairo', 'Lagos'] or [{ value, label }]

props.name: value
props.description: onChange receives the chosen value, not the typed text.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: onChange receives the chosen value, not the typed text.

props.name: onChange
props.description: onChange receives the chosen value, not the typed text.

props.name: emptyText
props.description: Shown when the typed text matches nothing.

keyboard.does: Open the list, then move through it.
Close the list; pressed again, clear the field.
Close the list and move on.

notes: The ARIA 1.2 list-autocomplete pattern: role combobox on the input, listbox beside it, no focus movement.
The part of each label that matched is marked.
The list is only in the page while there are matches, so aria-controls never points at nothing.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Combobox label="Time zone" options={zones} value={zone} onChange={setZone} />

entries.name: Field
entries.summary: The label, hint and error that every field shares, wired up so a screen reader hears them. The control you put inside it receives its id, aria-describedby and aria-invalid.
entries.description:
The label, hint and error every field shares, wired up so a screen reader
hears them: the control receives its id, `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid`
from the function passed as `children`.

<Field label="Email" hint="We reply from this address." error={error}>
 {(props) => <input {...props} type="email" />}
</Field>

An error replaces the hint, and is announced when it appears.

props.name: label
props.description: The visible label, tied to the control.

props.name: hint
props.description: Help text, read after the label. Replaced by the error while one is showing.

props.name: error
props.description: What is wrong. Announced as an alert when it appears.

props.name: children
props.description: Receives { id, aria-describedby, aria-invalid } and returns the control.

keyboard.does: Moves focus to the control it wraps; the label itself is not a stop.

notes: An error replaces the hint, so the described-by pointer never points at something that is not there.
Put all three props on the one element that takes focus.
Every other input in the kit is built on this.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Field label="Email" hint="We reply from this address." error={error} required>
  {(props) => <input {...props} type="email" />}
</Field>

entries.name: FileDrop
entries.summary: A drop zone that is also a file button: drag files onto it, or press it and choose. It lists what was picked and uploads nothing itself.

props.name: label
props.description: The two lines inside the zone.

props.name: hint
props.description: The two lines inside the zone.

props.name: accept
props.description: File types, as the input’s accept attribute.

props.name: onFiles
props.description: Called with an array of File objects.

keyboard.does: Open the file picker (the real input sits inside the zone).

notes: The list of chosen files is a polite live region.
Dragging gives a visual cue; the picker is always there for people who cannot or do not drag.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <FileDrop label="Choose files" accept=".csv" onFiles={(files) => read(files)} />

entries.name: NumberField
entries.summary: A number with a minus and a plus either side. The value is clamped to its range when you leave the field, never while you are typing.
entries.description:
A number with buttons either side. ↑ and ↓ step it, typing is free, and the
value is clamped to `min` and `max` when you leave the field — never while you
are typing, so "1" on the way to "12" is not rounded up to a minimum of 5.
`onChange` receives a number (or `null` while the field is empty).

props.name: value
props.description: onChange receives a number, or null while the box is empty.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: onChange receives a number, or null while the box is empty.

props.name: onChange
props.description: onChange receives a number, or null while the box is empty.

props.name: min
props.description: The range; the buttons stop at the ends.

props.name: max
props.description: The range; the buttons stop at the ends.

props.name: step
props.description: How much a press or an arrow key changes it; decimals are kept tidy.

keyboard.does: Step the value up or down.

notes: The plus and minus buttons are not tab stops: the arrow keys do their job for keyboard users.
Values are rounded to the precision of the step, so 1.25 + 0.05 is 1.3 and not 1.3000000000000003.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <NumberField label="Seats" min={1} max={12} value={n} onChange={setN} />

entries.name: PasswordField
entries.summary: A password field with a show/hide toggle and a rough strength meter. Everything happens in the page; nothing is sent anywhere.

keyboard.does: Moves to the show/hide button after the field.

notes: The meter scores length first and variety second and takes off common patterns; it is a nudge, not a guarantee.
The strength is written out in words as well as drawn, and announced politely.
autoComplete is “new-password” so password managers offer to generate one.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <PasswordField label="New password" hint="At least 12 characters is a good start." />

entries.name: RadioGroup
entries.summary: A group of real radio buttons under a legend: the arrow keys move and choose, Tab leaves the group, and a screen reader says “2 of 4”.

props.name: row
props.description: Lay the options out in a wrapping row.

keyboard.does: Move to the next or previous option and choose it.
Enter the group (on the chosen option) or leave it.

notes: Native radios in a fieldset: nothing to re-implement, nothing to get wrong.
Use Segmented when the choices are short and few and the control should look like one piece.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <RadioGroup legend="Support level" value={plan} onChange={setPlan} options={[{ value: 'self', label: 'Self-serve' }, { value: 'team', label: 'Team', hint: 'A named contact.' }]} />

entries.name: RangeField
entries.summary: A slider: the native range input, with its value written beside the label and a text version (“240 ms”) for assistive technology.

props.name: format
props.description: Turns the number into text for display and aria-valuetext.

props.name: marks
props.description: A few words under the track.

notes: Native, so touch dragging and keyboard control need no code of ours.
A slider is a poor way to enter an exact number — pair it with a NumberField where exactness matters.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <RangeField label="Duration" min={0} max={1000} step={20} value={ms} onChange={setMs} format={(n) => `${n} ms`} />

entries.name: SearchField
entries.summary: A search box with a clear button and, when you give it a count, a result count that is read out as it changes.

props.name: noun
props.description: What is being counted; the singular is made by dropping a trailing s.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: A hint inside the box — not a replacement for the label.

keyboard.does: Clears the box and keeps focus in it.

notes: It does not search anything itself; filter your own list from the text it gives you.
The count is a polite live region.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <SearchField label="Find a term" value={q} onChange={setQ} count={hits.length} noun="terms" />

entries.name: Segmented
entries.summary: A short row of exclusive choices drawn as one control, with an ink that glides to the chosen one. Radio buttons underneath.
entries.description:
A short row of exclusive choices drawn as one control, with an ink that glides
to the chosen one. Radio buttons underneath, so ← → choose, and it is named by
`label`. For choices that switch a panel of content, use Tabs.

options: ['Day', 'Week'] or [{ value, label }]

props.name: label
props.description: Names the group for assistive technology.

keyboard.does: Choose the previous or next segment.

notes: For choices that switch a panel of content, use Tabs. Segmented is for settings, not for pages.
Keep to two to five short options.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Segmented label="Range" options={['Day', 'Week', 'Month']} value={view} onChange={setView} />

entries.name: SelectField
entries.summary: A native select, styled. Native on purpose: the platform’s own keyboard handling, its picker on a phone and its screen-reader behaviour come for free.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: A disabled first option shown until something is chosen.

keyboard.does: Change the option (the platform’s own behaviour).
Jump to an option that starts with it.

notes: Use a Combobox when the list is long enough that people will want to type.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <SelectField label="Environment" options={['Development', 'Staging', 'Production']} />

entries.name: Switch
entries.summary: An on/off switch for a setting that takes effect at once. A button with role switch, so Space and Enter flip it and a screen reader says “on” or “off”.

props.name: label
props.description: The setting’s name; also the accessible name.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

notes: Use a checkbox for something that waits for a Save button; use a switch for something that happens as you flip it.
On and off are told apart by position and by a word, not only by colour.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Switch label="Email me when a deploy fails" checked={on} onChange={setOn} />

entries.name: TagInput
entries.summary: Type a word, press Enter or a comma and it becomes a tag. Each tag has its own remove button, and adding or removing is announced.

props.name: max
props.description: The most tags; the box is disabled once reached.

keyboard.does: Turn what you typed into a tag.
In an empty box, takes the last tag back.

notes: Duplicates (ignoring case) are refused with a spoken message.
Leaving the box with text in it adds the tag rather than losing the text.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <TagInput label="Topics" value={tags} onChange={setTags} max={6} />

entries.name: TextArea
entries.summary: A multi-line field that counts. Going over the limit turns the count red and marks the field invalid; it never cuts off what you typed.

props.name: maxLength
props.description: The most characters expected. Not enforced by truncation.

props.name: value
props.description: Controlled or uncontrolled; onChange receives the text.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Controlled or uncontrolled; onChange receives the text.

props.name: onChange
props.description: Controlled or uncontrolled; onChange receives the text.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

keyboard.does: Leaves the field (Tab is not a character here).

notes: The count is decorative; the over-the-limit message is announced as an alert.
The field can be resized vertically by the user.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <TextArea label="Describe the change" maxLength={140} hint="Two sentences is plenty." />

entries.name: TextField
entries.summary: A single-line text field with a label, hint and error, and an optional prefix and suffix inside the border for a currency, a unit or an @.

props.name: hint
props.description: Help text and the problem; see Field.

props.name: error
props.description: Help text and the problem; see Field.

props.name: prefix
props.description: Drawn inside the border, before and after the input.

props.name: suffix
props.description: Drawn inside the border, before and after the input.

props.name: type
props.description: Any input type that holds text.

props.name: ...input
props.description: Everything else goes to the input: value, defaultValue, onChange, placeholder, inputMode, readOnly, disabled.

keyboard.does: Moves into and out of the field.

notes: Controlled (value and onChange) or uncontrolled (defaultValue) — it is a plain input.
Autocomplete is off by default; turn it back on for names and addresses with the autoComplete attribute.
Disabled and read-only look different on purpose: read-only text can still be selected and copied.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <TextField label="Budget" prefix="$" suffix="per month" inputMode="numeric" value={v} onChange={(e) => setV(e.target.value)} />

entries.name: Breadcrumbs
entries.summary: Where you are, as a trail back up. The last item is the current page and is not a link.

props.name: items
props.description: { label, to? }. The last is the current page.

props.name: label
props.description: The nav landmark’s name; change it when two trails share a page.

keyboard.does: Through each link in the trail.

notes: An ordered list inside a nav, with aria-current on the last item; the separators are drawn by CSS and not read out.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Breadcrumbs items={[{ label: 'Resources', to: '/resources' }, { label: 'Glossary' }]} />

entries.name: DropdownMenu
entries.summary: A button that opens a menu of actions — not a navigation; use links for that. The ARIA menu-button pattern, with typeahead.
entries.description:
A button that opens a menu of actions (not a navigation: use links for that).
The ARIA menu-button pattern: ↓ or Enter opens and moves into the menu, ↑ ↓
Home End move, typing a letter jumps to the item that starts with it, Escape
closes and returns to the button, and Tab closes. A click elsewhere closes it.

items: [{ label, onSelect, danger?, disabled? } | { separator: true }]

props.name: label
props.description: The button’s text and the menu’s name.

props.name: items
props.description: { label, onSelect, danger?, disabled? } or { separator: true }.

props.name: align
props.description: Which edge of the button the menu lines up with.

keyboard.does: Open the menu and move to the first item.
Open and move to the last item.
Jump to the next item starting with it.
Close and return to the button.

notes: Focus moves into the menu when it opens and back to the button when it closes.
Disabled items are skipped by the arrow keys.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <DropdownMenu label="Actions" items={[{ label: 'Rename', onSelect: rename }, { separator: true }, { label: 'Delete…', onSelect: remove, danger: true }]} />

entries.name: OnThisPage
entries.summary: An “on this page” list that follows the reader: the entry for the section nearest the top is marked, and pressing one scrolls there and moves focus to it.
entries.description:
A "on this page" list that follows the reader: the item for the section
nearest the top of the screen is marked `aria-current="location"`. Clicking
one scrolls there (smoothly unless the reader prefers reduced motion) and moves
keyboard focus to the section, so the next Tab continues from it.

items: [{ id, label }]   — ids of elements on the page

props.name: items
props.description: { id, label } where id is an element on the page.

keyboard.does: Scroll to the section and focus it.

notes: Marked with aria-current="location".
Scrolling is instant for people who prefer reduced motion.
Focus moves to the section so the next Tab continues from it, rather than from the link.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <OnThisPage items={[{ id: 'intro', label: 'Introduction' }, { id: 'steps', label: 'Steps' }]} />

entries.name: Pagination
entries.summary: Page buttons with the first, the last and the neighbours of the current one, “…” for what is skipped, and previous and next that stop at the ends.

props.name: page
props.description: onChange receives the new page number.

props.name: defaultPage
props.description: onChange receives the new page number.

props.name: onChange
props.description: onChange receives the new page number.

props.name: siblings
props.description: How many neighbours to show each side of the current page.

keyboard.does: Through the buttons; Enter or Space presses one.

notes: The current page is aria-current and each button says “Page 6”, not just “6”.
A gap that stands for a single page is shown as that page instead of “…”.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Pagination page={page} pages={20} onChange={setPage} />

entries.name: SideNav
entries.summary: A vertical navigation in groups that fold. A folded group is out of the tab order and the reading order, not only out of sight.
entries.description:
A vertical navigation in groups that fold. A folded group is hidden from the
tab order and from screen readers, not only from the eye. The current item
carries `aria-current="page"`.

groups: [{ label, items: [{ label, to, badge? }], open? }]   current: the `to` of this page

props.name: groups
props.description: { label, items: [{ label, to, badge? }], open? }.

props.name: current
props.description: The `to` of the page you are on; it gets aria-current.

keyboard.does: Through the group buttons and the links of open groups.

notes: Group headings are real headings holding a button, so a screen reader can list them.
The first group starts open unless you say otherwise.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <SideNav current={pathname} groups={[{ label: 'Reliability', open: true, items: [{ label: 'Runbooks', to: '/insights/runbooks' }] }]} />

entries.name: Stepper
entries.summary: The steps of something with an order, and which one you are on. Done steps show a tick, the current one is aria-current, and each state is written out for a screen reader.
entries.description:
The steps of something with an order, and which one you are on. Done steps
show a tick, the current one is marked `aria-current="step"`, and each step's
state is also written out for a screen reader. On a phone it stacks.

steps: [{ title, hint? }]   current: the zero-based index

props.name: current
props.description: The zero-based index of the current step.

keyboard.does: A stepper shows progress; it is not a control. Put Back and Next buttons beside it.

notes: On a phone the steps stack and the connecting line is dropped.
It does not decide whether a step may be skipped — that rule belongs to your flow.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Stepper current={1} steps={[{ title: 'Details' }, { title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Confirm' }]} />

entries.name: Tabs
entries.summary: Tabs that change a panel of content, as the ARIA pattern asks: one tab stop for the list, arrow keys move between tabs and show the panel at once.
entries.description:
Tabs that change a panel of content, as the ARIA pattern asks: one tab stop
for the list, ← → (and Home, End) move between tabs and show the panel at once,
and the panel is a tab stop of its own if it has nothing focusable inside.
For choices that only change a nearby demo, use Segmented.

tabs: [{ id, label, content }]

props.name: value
props.description: The id of the selected tab.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: The id of the selected tab.

props.name: onChange
props.description: The id of the selected tab.

keyboard.does: Move to the previous or next tab, wrapping, and show its panel.
Leaves the list for the panel.

notes: Only for choices that switch a panel. A selector that changes a nearby demo is a radio group (Segmented).
The content of panels that are not shown is not rendered at all, and their panel element is hidden.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
…

}, { id: 'run', label: 'Running it', content:

…

}]} />

entries.name: Toolbar
entries.summary: A row of tool buttons that is one tab stop; the arrow keys move between the tools. A tool can be a toggle, with aria-pressed.
entries.description:
A row of tool buttons that is one tab stop: ← → (and Home, End) move between
the tools, as the ARIA toolbar pattern asks. A tool with `toggle` is a pressed/
not-pressed button and says so with `aria-pressed`.

items: [{ id, label, icon: LucideIcon, toggle?, pressed?, onClick? } | { separator: true }]

props.name: items
props.description: { id, label, icon?, toggle?, pressed?, onClick? } or { separator: true }.

notes: Icon-only tools get their name from the label, which is also their tooltip.
Roving tabindex: only the tool you last used is in the tab order.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Toolbar label="Text formatting" items={[{ id: 'b', label: 'Bold', icon: Bold, toggle: true }, { id: 'i', label: 'Italic', icon: Italic, toggle: true }]} />

entries.name: Alert
entries.summary: A message in the flow of the page. Information and success speak politely; warnings and errors interrupt. The tone is never carried by colour alone.

props.name: tone
props.description: Sets the icon, the colour and how it is announced.

props.name: onDismiss
props.description: Adds a dismiss button when given.

keyboard.does: To the dismiss button, if there is one.

notes: role="status" for info and success, role="alert" for warning and danger.
Do not auto-dismiss an alert; use a Toast for something that needs no answer.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Alert tone="warning" title="Token expires soon">Replace it before Friday.</Alert>

entries.name: Banner
entries.summary: A notice that runs the width of its container, for something about the whole page or site rather than one field. It may carry one action and may be dismissed.

props.name: action
props.description: { label, to } for a link or { label, onClick } for a button.

keyboard.does: To the action, then to the dismiss button.

notes: A group named by its title, so two banners on a page never collide as landmarks.
Dismissal lasts until the page is reloaded; nothing is stored.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Banner title="New:" action={{ label: 'Read the notes', to: '/resources/changelog' }}>A chapter was added to the release notes.</Banner>

entries.name: EmptyState
entries.summary: What a list or a page says when there is nothing in it: why it is empty, and the one thing to do next. An empty state with no way forward is a dead end.

props.name: action
props.description: The next step, usually a button.

notes: Say why it is empty — “nothing yet” and “nothing matches your filter” need different words.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <EmptyState icon={CalendarX2} title="Nothing scheduled" action={<button>Add the first one</button>}>When a job is scheduled it appears here.</EmptyState>

entries.name: Meter
entries.summary: A gauge for a quantity inside a known range. The colour changes in the low and high zones and the zone is also written out for anyone who cannot see the colour.
entries.description:
A gauge for a quantity inside a known range (disk used, budget spent) — not
progress toward a goal, which is a ProgressBar. Drawn as cells; the colour
changes in the low and high zones, and the zone is also written out for
anyone who cannot see the colour. `role="meter"` carries the numbers.

props.name: low
props.description: Below low or above high changes the zone.

props.name: high
props.description: Below low or above high changes the zone.

props.name: cells
props.description: How many cells to draw; the unit after the number.

props.name: unit
props.description: How many cells to draw; the unit after the number.

notes: role="meter" with min, max, now and a text value that includes the zone.
A meter is not progress toward a goal — that is a ProgressBar.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Meter label="Storage used" value={62} unit="%" low={10} high={85} />

entries.name: ProgressBar
entries.summary: How far along something is. With a value it announces its percentage; without one it is indeterminate and says it is working.

props.name: label
props.description: What is progressing; names the bar.

props.name: hideValue
props.description: Do not write the percentage beside the label.

notes: role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuetext and a name.
Indeterminate stops moving under reduced motion.
For a quantity in a range (storage used), use Meter.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<ProgressBar label="Importing rows" value={42} />
<ProgressBar label="Waiting for the server" />

entries.name: Skeleton
entries.summary: The shape of content that has not arrived yet, holding its space so nothing jumps when it does. Decorative: hidden from assistive technology.
entries.description:
The shape of content that has not arrived yet. Purely decorative, so it is
hidden from assistive technology — pair it with a live "loading" message
(a Spinner with `hideLabel`) wherever the wait matters.

<Skeleton width="60%" height="1rem" />      one block
<Skeleton lines={3} />                      a short paragraph

props.name: lines
props.description: Draw a short paragraph instead of one block; the last line is shorter.

notes: Pair it with a live “loading” message (a Spinner with hideLabel) wherever the wait matters.
The shimmer stops under reduced motion.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Skeleton width="48%" height="1.1rem" />
<Skeleton lines={3} />

entries.name: Spinner
entries.summary: A small “working on it” ring. It is a status message first — the label is announced — and a picture second. It stops turning for visitors who ask for less motion.

props.name: size
props.description: The ring’s size, as a CSS length.

props.name: hideLabel
props.description: Keep the label for screen readers only.

notes: If the wait is long enough to need a spinner, it is long enough to say what it is waiting for.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Spinner label="Saving" />
<Spinner label="Working" hideLabel />

entries.name: StatusDot
entries.summary: A coloured dot with its state spelled out beside it, so the colour is never the only signal. A live one can breathe.

props.name: state
props.description: Sets the colour and the default word.

props.name: pulse
props.description: A slow ring for a live thing; stops under reduced motion.

notes: The words are Operational, Degraded, Down and Idle unless you give your own.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<StatusDot state="ok" pulse />
<StatusDot state="warn" label="Slow responses" />

entries.name: ToastProvider
entries.summary: Brief messages in a corner that leave by themselves. Announced politely, never take focus, pause while the pointer or keyboard is on them, and can always be dismissed.
entries.description:
Brief messages that appear in a corner and leave by themselves. They are
announced politely in a live region, never take focus, pause while the pointer
or keyboard is on them, and can always be dismissed. A toast is for something
that needs no answer ("Copied"); anything that does is a dialog.

props.name: duration
props.description: Milliseconds before it leaves; 0 keeps it until dismissed.

props.name: max (provider)
props.description: How many show at once; older ones leave first.

keyboard.does: To a toast’s dismiss button; focusing a toast stops its timer.

notes: A toast is for something that needs no answer. Anything that does is a dialog.
Outside a provider, useToast returns a function that does nothing — so a component that toasts never has to know.

examples.title: Basic usage

entries.name: Avatar
entries.summary: A person, a team or a system as its initials in a circle or square. No photographs, on purpose: initials need no consent, load instantly and cannot be the wrong face.

props.name: name
props.description: The full name; becomes the accessible name.

props.name: names
props.description: The group shows max avatars and “+N” for the rest.

props.name: max (group)
props.description: The group shows max avatars and “+N” for the rest.

notes: The group lists every name in its accessible label, including those it only counts.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Avatar name="Alex Example" />
<AvatarGroup names={['Alex Example', 'Sam Sample', 'Rin Placeholder']} max={3} />

entries.name: AvatarGroup
entries.summary: Avatars stacked as one group, with a "+N" for the ones that do not fit.

entries.name: Badge
entries.summary: A short label for the state or kind of a thing: New, Beta, Deprecated. The word carries the meaning; the tone only reinforces it.

props.name: dot
props.description: A small mark before the word.

notes: Never use a badge’s colour alone to say something.
Keep it to one or two words.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Badge tone="success" dot>Healthy</Badge>

entries.name: BarList
entries.summary: Bars you can read as a list: each row has its label, a bar and the figure, so the values are text first and a picture second. The largest is picked out in red.

props.name: max
props.description: The value that fills a bar.

props.name: unit
props.description: Added after each value unless display is given.

notes: A list of items, so the order and the count are announced.
On a phone the bar drops under its label.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <BarList label="Jobs by owner" items={[{ label: 'Operations', value: 12 }, { label: 'Platform', value: 8 }]} />

entries.name: Chip
entries.summary: A compact pill that can be plain information, a toggle (give it onClick; selected says whether it is on) and/or removable (give it onRemove).

props.name: selected
props.description: Whether a toggle chip is on.

props.name: onClick
props.description: Makes it a toggle button with aria-pressed.

props.name: onRemove
props.description: Adds a separate close button named “Remove …”.

keyboard.does: Toggle, or press the remove button.

notes: A filter set is a group of toggle chips; name the group with role="group" and an aria-label.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Chip selected={on} onClick={toggle}>Operations</Chip>
<Chip onRemove={drop}>security</Chip>

entries.name: CodeBlock
entries.summary: A block of code with an optional file name, light colouring and a copy button. The colour is a nicety: every token is also plain text, so copying gives exactly what you see.
entries.description:
A block of code with an optional file name, light colouring and a copy button.
The colours are a nicety: every token is also plain text, so copying gives you
exactly what you see, and the block is a focusable region so a keyboard user
can scroll a long line. `lines` adds line numbers.

props.name: language
props.description: js, jsx, ts, json, css, sh, html or yaml; anything else is shown plain.

props.name: filename
props.description: Shown in the header; also names the region.

props.name: lines
props.description: Number the lines (the numbers are not copied).

keyboard.does: To the copy button, then into the code, so a long line can be scrolled with the arrow keys.

notes: The colouring is deliberately small — a tokenizer of about eighty lines, no dependency.
Copying uses the clipboard API, with a fallback for browsers that do not offer it.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <CodeBlock filename="retry.js" lines code={source} />

entries.name: DataTable
entries.summary: A table you can sort and select from. A sortable column’s header is a button and the th carries aria-sort. It scrolls sideways inside a focusable region on a narrow screen.
entries.description:
A table you can sort and select from. A sortable column's header is a button
and the `th` carries `aria-sort`; the first press sorts ascending, the second
descending, the third restores the original order. The table scrolls sideways
inside a focusable region on a narrow screen rather than breaking the page.

columns: [{ key, label, sortable?, align?: 'right', render?: (row) => node, value?: (row) => sortable }]

props.name: caption
props.description: The table’s caption and the region’s name.

props.name: columns
props.description: { key, label, sortable?, align?, render?, value? }.

props.name: rows
props.description: Objects; each needs a unique rowKey.

props.name: selectable
props.description: Adds checkboxes; onSelect receives the chosen keys.

props.name: onSelect
props.description: Adds checkboxes; onSelect receives the chosen keys.

props.name: maxHeight
props.description: Scroll vertically past this height; the header stays.

keyboard.does: On a header button: sort ascending, then descending, then back to the original order.
Into the scrolling region, then through its buttons and checkboxes.

notes: Sorting is stable and numeric-aware; numbers in a column should be right-aligned.
The header checkbox is indeterminate when only some rows are chosen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <DataTable caption="Scheduled jobs" rows={rows} selectable onSelect={setChosen} columns={[{ key: 'job', label: 'Job', sortable: true }, { key: 'mins', label: 'Minutes', sortable: true, align: 'right' }]} />

entries.name: DescriptionList
entries.summary: Terms and what they mean, or labels and their values — the right element for a fact sheet. A real dl, so a screen reader pairs each term with its detail.

props.name: items
props.description: { term, detail } — detail may be any node.

props.name: stacked
props.description: Put each detail under its term.

notes: On a phone every pair stacks.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <DescriptionList items={[{ term: 'Service', detail: 'Order intake' }, { term: 'Owner', detail: 'Commerce team' }]} />

entries.name: Sparkline
entries.summary: A tiny line chart with no axes, for “which way is it going”. It is an image with a text description — range, first and last value — so the shape is never the only way to learn it.

props.name: width
props.description: The viewBox; the chart scales to its container.

props.name: height
props.description: The viewBox; the chart scales to its container.

notes: The last point is marked.
Show the numbers somewhere nearby if they matter — a sparkline shows shape, not values.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Sparkline label="Response time" unit=" ms" data={[210, 190, 205, 180, 150, 140]} />

entries.name: Stat
entries.summary: One number, large, with its label above and, if you have it, how it moved. The change is written as words for a screen reader; the arrow and colour are decoration.

props.name: label
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: value
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: unit
props.description: The caption, the figure, and the small word after it.

props.name: change
props.description: Percent change; positive, negative or zero.

notes: Figures use lining numerals, so a 1 never looks like a capital I.
Say what a figure is compared with, or leave the change off.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Stat label="Jobs on time" value="96" unit="%" change={2} changeLabel="vs. last week" />

entries.name: Timeline
entries.summary: Things in the order they happen, down a line. It is an ordered list, so the order is announced. This site’s own timeline is told in undated phases — pass words, not dates, unless you have them.
entries.description:
Things in the order they happen, down a line. It is an ordered list, so the
order is announced; `when` can be a date, a phase or just "Step 3". Items with
`done` get a filled marker. The site's own timeline is told in undated phases —
pass words, not dates, unless you have them.

items: [{ when?, title, body?, done? }]
notes: Items marked done get a filled marker.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Timeline items={[{ when: 'Phase one', title: 'Shape', body: 'Work out the problem.', done: true }, { when: 'Phase two', title: 'Build' }]} />

entries.name: Tree
entries.summary: An expandable tree — files, categories, an outline — following the ARIA tree-view pattern: one tab stop, arrow keys through what is visible.
entries.description:
An expandable tree (files, categories, an outline), following the ARIA tree-view
pattern: one tab stop; ↑ ↓ move through what is visible; → opens a closed
branch or steps into an open one; ← closes it or steps out to the parent; Home
and End jump; Enter or Space chooses. `onSelect` receives the node.

nodes: [{ id, label, children?: [...] }]

props.name: nodes
props.description: { id, label, children? }, nested to any depth.

props.name: defaultOpen
props.description: Ids of branches that start open.

keyboard.does: Open a closed branch; on an open one, step into it.
Close an open branch; on a closed one or a leaf, step out to the parent.
Choose (and open or close) the item.

notes: aria-level, aria-setsize and aria-posinset are set, so a screen reader can say “3 of 5, level 2”.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Tree label="Project files" defaultOpen={['src']} onSelect={(node) => open(node.id)} nodes={[{ id: 'src', label: 'src', children: [{ id: 'main', label: 'main.jsx' }] }]} />

entries.name: ConfirmDialog
entries.summary: “Are you sure?” done properly: the title says what will happen, the buttons say what they do, and for something that cannot be undone the safe choice has focus.

props.name: danger
props.description: Red confirm button; focus starts on Cancel.

notes: Avoid “OK” and “Yes”: a button’s label should still make sense out of context.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <ConfirmDialog open={open} title="Delete this draft?" confirmLabel="Delete the draft" cancelLabel="Keep it" danger onConfirm={remove} onCancel={close}>It cannot be recovered.</ConfirmDialog>

entries.name: Dialog
entries.summary: A modal dialog: it takes over the screen until it is dealt with. Focus moves in and is trapped, Escape and the backdrop close it, the page behind stops scrolling and focus returns to what opened it.
entries.description:
A modal dialog: it takes over the screen until it is dealt with. Focus moves
in (to the element marked `data-autofocus`, else the first control), Tab and
Shift+Tab stay inside, Escape and a press on the backdrop close it, the page
behind stops scrolling, and focus returns to what opened it. It is named by
its title. Use it sparingly — most things do not need to interrupt.

<Dialog open={open} onClose={() => setOpen(false)} title="Rename" footer={<>…buttons…</>}>…</Dialog>

props.name: title
props.description: The heading; also the dialog’s name.

props.name: footer
props.description: The buttons; the primary action comes last.

props.name: dismissible
props.description: Allow Escape, the backdrop and the close button.

keyboard.does: Cycle through the controls inside; never leave.

notes: Mark the element that should take focus first with data-autofocus; otherwise it is the first control.
Smooth scrolling is stopped and the page behind is locked while it is open.
Use it sparingly — most things do not need to interrupt.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Dialog open={open} onClose={() => setOpen(false)} title="Rename" footer={<><button onClick={cancel}>Cancel</button><button onClick={save}>Save</button></>}>…</Dialog>

entries.name: Drawer
entries.summary: A dialog that slides in from an edge and runs the full height — for a filter panel or a record’s detail, where the page behind still gives context.
entries.description:
A dialog that slides in from an edge and runs the full height — for a filter
panel, a detail view, a settings sheet — where the page behind still gives
context. Everything a Dialog does for focus, Escape and scrolling, it does too.

<Drawer open={open} onClose={…} title="Filters" side="right">…</Drawer>

props.name: width
props.description: Its width, capped at the screen.

props.name: ...props
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

notes: Everything a Dialog does for focus, Escape and scrolling, a Drawer does too.
Under reduced motion it appears without sliding.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Drawer open={open} onClose={close} title="Filters" side="right">…</Drawer>

entries.name: HoverCard
entries.summary: A preview card for a link: hover or focus the link and a little more about where it goes appears, and stays while the pointer is on it. It must only ever add.
entries.description:
A preview card for a link: hover or focus the link and a little more about where
it goes appears, and stays while the pointer is on it. Because touch has no
hover, the card must only ever *add* — the link has to make sense without it.

<HoverCard title="Glossary" body="Every term the site uses…"><Link to="/resources/glossary">…</Link></HoverCard>

props.name: delay
props.description: Milliseconds of hover before it opens.

keyboard.does: Focusing the link opens the card.

notes: Touch has no hover, so the link has to make sense without the card.
Linked by aria-describedby; the card is not focusable.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <HoverCard title="Glossary" body="Every term the site uses…"><Link to="/resources/glossary">glossary</Link></HoverCard>

entries.name: Popover
entries.summary: A panel that opens under a button and holds anything — text, a small form, a few links. It is not modal: focus stays where it is and Tab moves on into the panel.
entries.description:
A panel that opens under a button and holds anything — text, a small form, a
few links. It is not modal: focus stays where it is and Tab moves on into the
panel, which follows the button in the page. Escape closes it and returns to the
button; so does a press anywhere outside.

props.name: title
props.description: A small heading inside the panel; also names it.

keyboard.does: Close and return to the button.
Into the panel, which follows the button in the page.

notes: A press outside closes it.
If it must be answered before anything else, it is a dialog, not a popover.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Popover label="Share" title="Share this view">…</Popover>

entries.name: Tooltip
entries.summary: A short description that appears beside a control on hover or keyboard focus, after a beat so it does not flicker. It adds detail; it never replaces a label.
entries.description:
A short description that appears beside a control on hover or keyboard focus,
after a beat so it does not flicker as the pointer crosses. It is wired up with
`aria-describedby`, is dismissed with Escape, and never holds anything the user
needs to act on — a tooltip adds detail, it does not replace a label.

<Tooltip text="Copy a link"><button>…</button></Tooltip>   (one focusable child)

props.name: delay
props.description: Milliseconds of hover before it shows (focus shows it at once).

keyboard.does: Focusing the control shows the tooltip.

notes: Wired with aria-describedby on the one focusable child.
Never put anything in a tooltip the user needs to act on — touch has no hover.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Tooltip text="Copy a link"><button aria-label="Copy a link">…</button></Tooltip>

entries.name: AspectRatio
entries.summary: Reserves a box of a fixed shape and fills it with its child, so an image, a video or a chart has its room before it loads and nothing below it jumps.
notes: The child is stretched to fill, so give media object-fit.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <AspectRatio ratio="16 / 9"><iframe title="…" /></AspectRatio>

entries.name: Callout
entries.summary: A remark set apart from the text around it: a note, a tip, a warning. The kind is written out as a word as well as shown by colour and icon.

props.name: tone
props.description: Icon, colour and the default title word.

notes: A note role, not a landmark and not an alert — it is part of the reading flow, so a page can have as many as it needs.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Callout tone="warning">Changing the retention period applies to new records only.</Callout>

entries.name: Card
entries.summary: A surface that groups related content, in four variants. The title is a heading whose level you choose, so the card fits the outline of the page it is on.
entries.description:
A surface that groups related content. Variants: `raised` (the default),
`flat`, `outline` and `accent`. The title is a heading whose level you choose
with `as`, so the card fits the outline of the page it is on. `interactive`
lifts it on hover and focus — put the one link or button inside it, and make
that the thing you press (do not wrap a whole card in a link).

props.name: eyebrow
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

props.name: title
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

props.name: footer
props.description: The small label, the heading and the foot line.

keyboard.does: To the one link or button inside it.

notes: Do not wrap a whole card in a link — put the link on the title or in the footer.
Use the accent variant at most once per screen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Card eyebrow="Accent" title="Pick one" variant="accent" footer="Once per screen.">The red wash says start here.</Card>

entries.name: Center
entries.summary: A capped column, centred in its parent — for a form, a card or a short passage. Fills the parent on a phone, stops at `max` on a desktop. New in this library.

props.name: max
props.description: The widest it gets. rem reads best: 36rem = 576 px.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

bestPractices.text: Use it instead of `margin: auto` and a fixed width.

rules: capped: width = min(parent, max).

examples.title: Basic
examples.code: <Center max="36rem"><Card title="Sign in">…</Card></Center>

entries.name: Cluster
entries.summary: Children in a row that wraps when it runs out of room — buttons, tags, links.
notes: Reading order is source order — wrapping never reorders anything.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Cluster gap={3} justify="space-between"><Chip>…</Chip><Chip>…</Chip></Cluster>

entries.name: Container
entries.summary: The page width: centred, 1360 px max (gutters included), with a fluid 20–80 px gutter. size="text" narrows it to a 760 px reading column. New in this library — the same as the global `.container` class.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

bestPractices.text: One Container per Section, directly inside it.
Nest Containers: the gutters double.

rules: Content width: 320 / 691 / 1152 / 1200 px at 360 / 768 / 1280 / 1920 viewports.

examples.title: Basic
examples.code: <Container size="text"><Prose>…</Prose></Container>

entries.name: Disclosure
entries.summary: One section that opens and closes — a question and its answer, a “more detail”. The closed body is out of the tab order and the reading order, not only out of sight.
entries.description:
One section that opens and closes — a question and its answer, a "more detail".
The heading holds a button that says whether the section is open; the closed
body is out of the tab order and the reading order, not only out of sight.
Several in a row make an accordion; the fx/Accordion adds numbering and motion.

props.name: title
props.description: The heading’s text; the button inside it opens and closes.

notes: Several in a row make an accordion. The fx Accordion adds numbering and a scrambling code.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Disclosure title="What does idempotent mean?" defaultOpen>Doing it twice has the same effect as once.</Disclosure>

entries.name: Divider
entries.summary: A line between things. Without a label it is a plain thematic break; with one it reads as a section break (“or”, “Later”) and is a separator, not a heading.

props.name: children
props.description: An optional word in the middle.

notes: Decorative breaks should be CSS, not elements; use a Divider when the break means something.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
<Divider />
<Divider>or</Divider>

entries.name: Figure
entries.summary: Something visual with a caption. The caption belongs to the figure, so a screen reader reads the two together.
notes: Whatever goes inside needs its own text alternative: an alt, or an aria-label on an SVG.

examples.title: Basic usage

entries.name: Grid
entries.summary: Children in as many equal columns as fit, none narrower than a minimum. There is no breakpoint to maintain: on a phone the minimum is wider than the screen, so you get one column.

props.name: min
props.description: The narrowest a column may be.

notes: Uses auto-fit with min(100%, …) so a column never overflows a narrow screen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Grid min="15rem" gap={4}>{cards}</Grid>

entries.name: Heading
entries.summary: A heading in the serif voice. `level` is the HTML element (for the outline); `size` is how it looks, from the type scale — display, hero, h1–h4. New in this library.
entries.description:
A heading in the serif voice. `level` is the HTML element (h1–h6, for the
outline); `size` is how it looks, from the type scale:
'display' · 'hero' · 'h1' · 'h2' · 'h3' · 'h4'. They are separate on purpose:
the outline is about structure, the size is about the design.
Sizes are fluid tokens (`--fs-*`): never set a font size on it.

props.name: ...rest
props.description: Everything else is passed to the root element.

bestPractices.text: One `level={1}` per page; keep levels in order.
Set a font size, weight or colour on it.

rules: Block-level; fluid type (`--fs-*`). Wraps balanced; cap very long titles with a Container or `Center`.

examples.title: Basic
examples.code: <Heading level={1} size="hero">Operational platforms.</Heading>

entries.name: Prose
entries.summary: A reading column. Wrap plain HTML — headings, paragraphs, lists, links, code, quotes — and it is typeset for reading: about 68 characters wide, generous leading, serif headings.
notes: Links are underlined — colour is not the only cue — and the underline turns red on hover.
Lines stay around 68 characters wide on any screen.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code:
Handing a system over

…

  • …

entries.name: Quote
entries.summary: A pull quote with its source: a real blockquote inside a figure, the attribution as the caption. Only put words here that someone really said.

props.name: cite
props.description: Who said it, or where it is from.

notes: This site quotes its own principles, not testimonials — nothing invented, nothing implied.

examples.title: Basic usage
examples.code: <Quote cite="From this company’s principles">A system that is hard to hand over is hard to trust.</Quote>

entries.name: Section
entries.summary: A page block's outer shell: the vertical rhythm between blocks (80–176 px, or 48–96 px with size="sm"). New in this library — the same as the global `.section` class.
entries.description:
A page block's outer shell: the vertical rhythm between blocks.

size   'md' (default) --section-pad, 80–176 px top and bottom
      'sm'           --section-pad-sm, 48–96 px (related blocks that read as one)
      'none'         no padding (the block pads itself)

Put a `Container` inside. Never add padding or margin of your own.

props.name: ...rest
